subject: expressions on LHS of sampling statements

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: expressions on LHS of sampling statements
parts:
I just committed changes to Stan to allow
general expressions on the LHS of sampling
statements. This should save some derived
data and parameter definitions and (I hope)
make the models easier to read.

The general form for sampling statements is now:

expr ~ distribution(expr[1],...,expr[N]);

This means we can do things like write:

1 ~ bernoulli(theta);

instead of what we'd have to do in BUGS:

x <- 1
x ~ bernoulli(theta);

Similarly, if we want the binomial prior from
BDA (which I know Andrew doesn't like any more), we
could write:

a / (a + b) ~ uniform(0,1);
a + b ~ pareto(1.5,0.5);
for (n in 1:N)
theta[n] ~ beta(a,b);

instead of:

phi ~ uniform(0,1);
kappa ~ pareto(1.5,0.5);
a <- kappa * phi;
b <- kappa * (1 - phi);
for (n in 1:N)
theta[n] ~ beta(a,b);

- Bob

messages.author: ab7b24da45678eac
messages.subject: Re: expressions on LHS of sampling statements
parts:
I have some doubts about this. It looks to me
the LHS is directly plugged into the "log-posterior",
which is not correct to me. Where is the Jacobian?

For example, we would think the following two
are equivalent:

// model I
model {
y ~ gamma(3, 2);
}

// model 2
model {
(1 / y ) ~ inv_gamma(3, 2);
}

However, if we just plug in (1/y) into
the inverse gamma's pdf,
we end up specifying y ~ gamma(5, 2).

Additionally, when I am building Bugs examples,
I noticed that we could can specify prior on
derived parameters. I am wondering
how that is dealt with. An example is
the following model (only part of it):

parameters {
double(0,) sigma;
}

derived parameters {
double(0,) tau;
tau <- 1 / square(sigma);
}

model {
tau ~ gamma(.001, .001);
}

--
Jiqiang

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Jacobians and lp__ += vs. ~
parts:
On 12/11/11 1:15 PM, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
> I have some doubts about this. It looks to me
> the LHS is directly plugged into the "log-posterior",
> which is not correct to me. Where is the Jacobian?

Thanks! You're absolutely right -- my suggestion
was totally buggy.

It's only safe to transform the left-hand-side of a
twiddle (sample) operator if it's all data. That's
the equivalent of BUGS's odd combo:

x <- ...
x ~ ...

JAGS makes you do data transforms in a separate block,
and that's also possible, but not required, in Stan.

Jiaqiang's correction made me realize that we can encode
the Jacobians directly with no problem in Stan.

> we could can specify prior on
> derived parameters.

> double(0,) sigma;
> }
>
> derived parameters {
> double(0,) tau;
> tau<- 1 / square(sigma);
> }
>
> model {
> tau ~ gamma(.001, .001);
> }

The way to think about Stan is that:

a ~ foo(b,c);

is just a convenient way to write

lp__ = lp__ + foo_log(a,b,c);

where lp__ is the running total log probability
and foo_log is the log probability function for Foo.

(Now that we have type checking, I need to add
in "lp__" as a known variable before this'll work --
I'll post a note when I do that later.)

So your example just reduces to:

pow(sigma,-2) ~ gamma(1E-3,1E-3);

And as you point out, we're still missing the Jacobian.

You can add that back in by:

pow(sigma,-2) ~ gamma(1E-3,1E-3);
lp__ = lp__ + log(abs(-2 * pow(sigma,-3));

Stan will also let you write the whole model this
way and not use any ~ at all, replacing the above with:

lp__ = lp__ + gamma_log(pow(sigma,-2), 1E-3, 1E-3);
lp__ = lp__ + log(abs(-2 * pow(sigma,-3));

This is making me think I should implement the +=
operator, at least.

In general, if we transform, we also need the log
absolute derivative added in:

g(y) ~ foo(...);
lp__ = lp__ + log(abs(g'(y))

where g'(y) is the derivative of the transform.

If y is multivariate, you need the whole log absolute
determinant of the Jacobian:

log(abs(determinant(Jacobian(g)))

Automating this all with auto-dif would require second
order auto-dif, because we still need to differentiate
the final lp__ w.r.t. the parameters.

Maybe for Stan 2.0. It's the same second order extension
we'll need to do Hessians via auto-dif.

- Bob
